title: One form, many sights
hookLine: ek moorat anek darsan: one form seen in countless ways (Jaap, roaaval)

lines: A DRAGON, A PRINCESS, A TALKING CAT.
THE BOOK CLOSES: ONE VOICE AGAIN.
cards: Bedtime, and a parent is reading a story out loud. The dragon gets a deep growl, the princess a bright, quick voice, and the old king, the narrator and the talking cat each sound different.

The child in bed believes every one of them. Nothing came from outside: all those voices were in one person the whole time. Then the book closes, the light goes off, and there's just one voice again, saying goodnight.
Many from one, and back to one. Jaap Sahib has a stanza that works like that.

teach.b: In a meter called roaal, with longer, rolling lines, one stanza opens: ek moorat anek darsan, keen roop anek. Ek is one. Moorat is form or likeness.

Anek is many, countless. Darsan is a sight, a glimpse, the word Sikhs use for seeing something holy, as when people go for darshan at the Golden Temple. One form, countless sights; You made forms beyond number.
Then: khel khel akhel khelan, ant ko phir ek. Khel is play, a game. Having played the play, beyond all play, at the end, again One.
Earlier, Jaap called the One aroop, formless. Now it says the One shows itself in countless forms. Sikh readers don't hear a contradiction.
Think of the reader at bedtime: no dragon's growl of their own, and yet every voice in the story is theirs.

teach.h: KHEL: THE WORLD AS THE ONE'S PLAY.
teach.b: Sikh scripture often calls the world the One's khel, the great unfolding game: in that reading, every person, every animal, every grain of sand is one more voice in the same story.

teach.h: ANT KO PHIR EK: AT THE END, ONE.
teach.b: And then the book closes, and it all folds back.
Again, One. That reading can change how people look at each other.
The rude driver, your sister, the stranger on the bus, the friend you think you know completely: each a different voice from the same source, and none of them the whole picture of anyone.

how: Sikhs recite this roaal stanza of Jaap Sahib each morning, and the idea of the world as the One's khel, play, runs through Sikh scripture and kirtan.

o: one way of life that suits everyone
the One, showing itself in countless forms
a single statue that stands for God

games.q: one form, many sights — tap the pairs.

s: one form, many sights contradicts aroop, formless
Sikh readers hold both: the One has no form of its own, and every form is its play.
darsan is the word for seeing something holy
as when people go for darshan at the Golden Temple.
the stanza ends with everything staying many
khel khel akhel khelan, ant ko phir ek: at the end, again One.

games.q: the One has made forms beyond number and played the great play. what does the stanza say happens at the end?
o: the play starts over the same way.
games.why: ant ko phir ek: having played the play, beyond all play, at the end it all folds back into One.

practice: Picture someone you know well, then see them from angles you usually don't: as a small child, as their parents see them, at three in the morning, on their best day.
Let each picture be one more voice in their story, then let them fold back into the one person. If you pray, you can say ek moorat anek darsan softly.

wordCard.voice: One form. Ek moorat anek darsan: one form, seen in countless ways, playing the great play and at the end, again One.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: moorat, form or likeness; ek moorat, one form, as in akaal moorat in the Mool Mantar.

carryVoice: Your line: one, seen many ways. None of those sights is the whole picture. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Jaap Sahib, roaal chhand (around stanza 81): ek moorat anek darsan keen roop anek / khel khel akhel khelan ant ko phir ek
